response.answer: Price elasticities typically range from -2.8 to -0.7; enforcement elasticity and catchability are not standardly defined. Prioritize price elasticity for sensitivity analysis due to its direct impact on revenue.

results.title: What will happen when we raise our price? (How to Apply Price Elasticity)
results.content: (How to Apply Price Elasticity)**. (How to Apply Price Elasticity). Things to know about price elasticity for the vast majority of CPG products:. * Price elasticity is always negative. * Consumers’ sensitivity to price changes (what elasticity is measuring) is affected by many different things. * Based on my 30+ years of experience across LOTS of product categories, price elasticity is usually something between about -2.8 and -0.7. (IRI and NielsenIQ have both shared research that shows price elasticities have changed very little, even during the last couple of years.)  The larger the elasticity is in absolute value the more sensitive consumers are to a price change. We recently received a question from a reader asking about which of 2 different formulas they should use to estimate the volume of a price increase, given that they know the product’s price elasticity. * Elasticity -2.8 (consumers are very sensitive to price changes for this product!). So this shows that a price increase of +15% on a product that is very elastic is likely to result in a volume decline of 42%. Depending on what the price elasticity is the volume increase could be huge! Always thought elasticity is estimate as % in volume/ a 1% change in price. A quality elasticity model should be able to express cross-elasticity, price thresholds and have software that’s both easy to use and can let you do both quick calculations and – as you’ll inevitably end up doing – trade plans. There are some variations for how to apply the price elasticity. Most people looking for quick and dirty are applying a formula to *average* price, when in theory the price elasticity should be applied to base price and “supplemented” with promotion multipliers and lift by tactic. Quick Question – Why should we apply pricing elasticity on base price and not on actual price ? And how do we calculate promo price elasticity ? Unless you are able to get data that measures how much consumers/shoppers are buying and at what price you really cannot get to a true price elasticity. You also want to be careful about what else was happening at the same time that price was changing so that you don’t over- or under-estimate the price elasticity.

results.title: The Science (and Art) of Estimating Price Elasticities | by Armin Kakas | Medium
results.content: Quantitatively, companies express customer (either B2B or B2C) price sensitivity with **price elasticity**, and the modeling of accurate price elasticity coefficients is still one of the most popular data science use cases in sales and marketing (and, of course, revenue management) domains. In this article, I will describe the most popular analytical methods that help you measure your product or service price elasticities, including a few simple and proven ML-based approaches that your analytics or data science teams can easily do. ML-based approaches work well if you want to understand price elasticities for well-established products with at least 2–3 years of sales history, including competitive pricing trends. ## What are the best modeling approaches to estimate Price Elasticity in my industry? Ensemble Models allow you to quickly estimate Elasticities across various Price Ranges and Customer Segments - since we know that P/E slopes often vary. If you use ML-based customer survey approaches, confirm those price elasticity estimates with well-designed in-market tests to understand price changes’ real, empirical impacts.

results.title: Oil price elasticities and oil price fluctuations - ScienceDirect
results.content: Studies identifying oil shocks using structural vector autoregressions (VARs) reach different conclusions on the relative importance of supply and demand factors in explaining oil market fluctuations. When the estimated elasticities are embedded into a structural VAR, supply and demand shocks play an equally important role in explaining oil prices and oil quantities. Our starting point is to show how the cross-equation restrictions that are inherent in standard VARs of the oil market impose an inverse, nonlinear relation between the short-run price elasticities of oil supply and demand. In particular, with a configuration of the oil market characterized by a zero supply elasticity, all movements in oil prices are attributed to oil-specific demand shocks. By contrast, setting the supply elasticity to 0.1 implies that oil supply and oil demand shocks are equally important drivers of oil price fluctuations. Second, we propose a novel way of selecting oil supply and demand elasticities in a manner that combines external information from country-specific oil supply shocks with the cross-equations restrictions that are inherent in a just-identified VAR model.5 Kilian and Murphy(2012), Lippi and Nobili(2012), and Baumeister and Hamilton(2017) embed prior distributions for the elasticities in structural VARs of the oil market in order to identify shocks to oil supply and demand. Similarly, our estimates of the oil demand elasticity are in line with existing empirical studies.6 Finally, our approach of combining country-specific data on oil production with an aggregate VAR echoes the approach of the global VAR (GVAR) literature pioneered by Dees et al.(2007) and Mohaddes and Pesaran(2016). We set the weights matrix _V_ in Eq.(10) to be diagonal, with the entries equal to the variances associated with the point Using external information from a large panel of countries, we impose restrictions on the short-run price elasticities of oil supply and oil demand in order to identify a structural VAR model of the global oil market. My analysis reaffirms the conclusion that the one-month oil supply elasticity is close to zero, which implies that oil demand shocks are the dominant driver of the real price of oil.

results.title: Oil price elasticities and oil price fluctuations - ScienceDirect
results.content: Studies identifying oil shocks using structural vector autoregressions (VARs) reach different conclusions on the relative importance of supply and demand factors in explaining oil market fluctuations. When the estimated elasticities are embedded into a structural VAR, supply and demand shocks play an equally important role in explaining oil prices and oil quantities. In this paper, we assess the relative importance of supply and demand factors in explaining oil market fluctuations, and find that supply and demand shocks are equally important in accounting for fluctuations in oil prices and oil quantities. Our starting point is to show how the cross-equation restrictions that are inherent in standard VARs of the oil market impose an inverse, nonlinear relation between the short-run price elasticities of oil supply and demand. In particular, with a configuration of the oil market characterized by a zero supply elasticity, all movements in oil prices are attributed to oil-specific demand shocks. By contrast, setting the supply elasticity to 0.1 implies that oil supply and oil demand shocks are equally important drivers of oil price fluctuations. In order to estimate oil supply and demand elasticities, we combine narrative analysis with instrumental-variable regressions for a large panel of countries. Second, we propose a novel way of selecting oil supply and demand elasticities in a manner that combines external information from country-specific oil supply shocks with the cross-equations restrictions that are inherent in a just-identified VAR model.5. Kilian and Murphy (2012), Lippi and Nobili (2012), and Baumeister and Hamilton (2017) embed prior distributions for the elasticities in structural VARs of the oil market in order to identify shocks to oil supply and demand. Similarly, our estimates of the oil demand elasticity are in line with existing empirical studies.6 Finally, our approach of combining country-specific data on oil production with an aggregate VAR echoes the approach of the global VAR (GVAR) literature pioneered by Dees et al. This section provides empirical evidence about the price elasticity of global supply and demand for crude oil by estimating instrumental variable (IV) panel regressions. Using external information from a large panel of countries, we impose restrictions on the short-run price elasticities of oil supply and oil demand in order to identify a structural VAR model of the global oil market.
